Module 4: full concept tree
Top umbrella term at the top, details below it. Everything shown is from your PPT.
IP level security Transport level security Email security
Module 4
IP Security,
Transport Level
Security &
Email Security
IP Level Security
(IPSec)
What it is
Protocols by IETF that
secure packets at the
network (IP) layer
Why security at IP
layer?
App-layer security
covers only some apps
(PGP, S/MIME = email
only)
Some apps use UDP, so
SSL/TLS (needs TCP)
can't protect them
Routing protocols use IP
directly
Applications
Secure branch-office
connectivity
Secure remote access
Extranet / intranet with
partners
Safer e-commerce
Services (RFC
4301)
Access control
Message integrity
Entity authentication
Rejection of replayed
packets
Confidentiality
Modes of
operation
Transport mode
Protects only the IP payload,
not the IP header
Host-to-host (end-to-end)
Lower overhead
AH: authenticates payload +
parts of header
ESP: encrypts payload (not
header)
Tunnel mode
Protects the entire IP packet,
adds a new IP header
Gateway-to-gateway, VPNs
More overhead
AH: authenticates inner
packet + parts of outer
header
ESP: encrypts entire inner
packet incl. its header
Protection
mechanisms
(sub-protocols)
AH
Authentication
Header
Source authentication +
integrity, NO privacy
IP protocol field = 51
Header fields
Next header
Payload length
SPI (Security Parameter
Index)
Sequence number (stops
replay)
Authentication data (hash)
ESP
Encapsulating
Security Payload
Authentication + integrity +
privacy
IP protocol field = 50
Adds header + trailer; auth
data at the end
Steps: add trailer, encrypt,
add header, compute auth
data, add IP header
Key components
SA
Security Association
Logical connection between
two endpoints
Holds: protocols, algorithms,
keys, lifetime
Identified by the SPI
IKE
Internet Key
Exchange
Negotiates, establishes and
manages SAs
Functions: authentication,
key generation, SA setup, SA
management
Phase 1: secure channel
(public-key auth)
Phase 2: negotiate SA
parameters
IPSec
Architecture
(documents)
Architecture
ESP protocol
AH protocol
Encryption algorithm
Authentication
algorithm
DOI (Domain of
Interpretation)
Key management
Transport Level
Security
Web security
considerations
WWW = client/server
over TCP/IP, so it is
vulnerable
Approaches: IP level
(IPSec), Transport level
(SSL/TLS), Application
level
Need of transport
level security
Entity authentication
Message integrity
Confidentiality
SSL
Secure Sockets
Layer
Netscape, 1994; latest
= SSLv3
Connection vs
Session
Connection: transient,
peer-to-peer, tied to one
session
Session: client-server
association made by
Handshake, shared by many
connections
SSL Protocol Stack
(2 layers, 4
protocols)
Upper layer
Handshake Protocol
Negotiates cipher suite,
authenticates parties, builds
secrets
Done in 4 phases
ChangeCipherSpec
Protocol
Moves pending state to
active state (1-byte
message)
Alert Protocol
Reports errors, 2 bytes: level
(warning 1 / fatal 2) + code
Lower layer
Record Protocol
(carries everything)
Services: message integrity
(MAC) + confidentiality
(encryption)
Steps: fragment (2^14 B),
compress (optional), MAC,
encrypt, add header
Header: content type, major
ver, minor ver, compressed
length
Key exchange
methods (6)
NULL
RSA
Anonymous DH
Ephemeral DH
Fixed DH
Fortezza
Cipher suite
= key exchange +
encryption + hash algorithm
e.g.
SSL_DHE_RSA_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA
TLS
Transport Layer
Security
IETF standard version
of SSL (TLS 1.0 ~
SSLv3)
Differences from SSL
No Fortezza, so 5
key-exchange methods
Alerts: no NoCertificate,
some new ones added
Handshake: CertificateVerify
and Finished hashes
simplified
Record layer: HMAC, with
protocol version added
Cryptographic secret
generation
Building blocks
Data-expansion function
(HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1)
PRF = secret + label + seed
(MD5 XOR SHA-1
expansions)
Flow
1. Pre-master secret (same
as SSL)
2. Master secret (label
"master secret")
3. Key material (label "key
expansion")
HTTPS
(HTTP + SSL/TLS)
Uses https:// and port
443 (HTTP uses 80)
Encrypted: URL,
content, forms, cookies,
HTTP headers
Start: TLS Client Hello,
handshake, then HTTP
request
Close: close_notify
alert, then TCP closes
SSH
Secure Shell
Secure network
communication, simple
and inexpensive
Email Security
Background
RFC 5322 (SMTP
format)
Header lines, blank line, then
body
Keywords: From, To, Subject,
Date
SMTP limitations
No binary / executable files
No national language
characters
Size limits
ASCII-EBCDIC mapping and
X.400 gateway problems
MIME
Multipurpose
Internet Mail
Extensions
5 header fields
MIME-Version
Content-Type
Content-Transfer-Encoding
Content-ID
Content-Description
Content types: 7 major,
15 subtypes
Transfer encodings
7bit, 8bit, binary (no
encoding done)
quoted-printable
base64 (radix-64)
x-token
Native vs canonical
form
S/MIME
Secure MIME
Security enhancement
to MIME (RSA Data
Security)
Uses
application/pkcs7-mime
content type
CMS data content
types
Signed-data: integrity
(signature)
Enveloped-data: privacy
Digested-data: integrity
Encrypted-data: no recipient,
for storage
Authenticated-data:
authentication (MAC)
Functionality
Enveloped data
Signed data
Clear-signed data
Signed and enveloped data
Algorithms
Digital signature: DSS
Session key encryption:
Diffie-Hellman / ElGamal
Message encryption: Triple
DES
Public-key certificates
signed by CAs

OSI model vs TCP/IP model: protocols at each layer
Same protocols on both sides. Layers line up row by row, so you can see which OSI layers each TCP/IP layer covers.

DNS DHCP Telnet SSH SNMP S/MIME

* SSL/TLS: your PPT (slide 38) draws it as a security layer between Application and Transport. Many textbooks place it at the OSI Presentation layer, as drawn here.
Physical layer items are standards and media, not protocols. Protocol placement can differ slightly between textbooks.
